title: A Personalised Cancer Vaccine Just Kept Melanoma Away for Five Years. The Technology Behind It Could Change Everything.
excerpt: Moderna and Merck's mRNA vaccine, custom-built from each patient's tumour DNA, cut the risk of recurrence by 49 per cent in the longest follow-up of any individualized cancer treatment ever tested.
body:
A personalized mRNA cancer vaccine developed by Moderna and Merck has achieved what no individualized cancer treatment has managed before: five years of sustained protection against one of the deadliest forms of skin cancer.

Data presented at the 2026 American Society of Clinical Oncology Annual Meeting showed that intismeran autogene — an mRNA-based therapy custom-built from each patient's tumour DNA — combined with the immunotherapy drug Keytruda reduced the risk of melanoma recurrence or death by 49 per cent compared to Keytruda alone. The risk of the cancer spreading to distant organs dropped by 59 per cent.

The numbers are striking enough on their own. But the real significance lies in the durability. At the three-year mark, the combination was already showing promise. Now, at five years, the protection has not only held but strengthened.

## How a Vaccine Gets Built From Your Own Tumour

Unlike traditional vaccines that target a single known pathogen, intismeran autogene is manufactured individually for each patient. After a tumour is surgically removed, its DNA is sequenced to identify up to 34 unique mutations — called neoantigens — that distinguish the cancer from healthy tissue. A single synthetic mRNA strand encoding those neoantigens is then produced and injected, training the patient's immune system to hunt down any remaining cancer cells carrying those exact signatures.

The process takes about six to eight weeks from biopsy to first dose. Patients in the trial received nine doses of the vaccine alongside standard Keytruda immunotherapy.

"This is the first demonstration of efficacy for an investigational mRNA cancer treatment in a randomized clinical trial," said Dr Stephen Hoge, president of Moderna. The FDA has granted the therapy breakthrough designation, and a larger Phase 3 confirmatory trial is already enrolling patients.

## Why South Asians Should Pay Attention

Melanoma has long been considered a disease of fair-skinned populations, and that assumption has had consequences. South Asians are diagnosed at later stages, when the cancer is harder to treat, partly because neither patients nor physicians are screening for it. A 2024 study in the *Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology* found that melanoma survival rates for South Asian patients lag significantly behind those for white patients, primarily due to delayed detection.

The mRNA vaccine platform is not limited to melanoma. Moderna and Merck are already testing the same approach in non-small cell lung cancer, and the technology can theoretically be adapted to any solid tumour with identifiable neoantigens. For a population with elevated genetic risk for certain cancers — including gallbladder, oral, and cervical cancers — this platform could eventually become a cornerstone of post-surgical treatment.

## What This Means for the Diaspora

For NRIs watching from the United States, the practical implications are both medical and financial. Moderna's stock surged after the ASCO presentation, and the personalized oncology market is projected to reach $15 billion by 2030. But the more immediate question is access.

The vaccine is not yet approved. The Phase 3 INTerpath-001 trial is actively recruiting at cancer centres across the US, UK, and Australia. Indian Americans with high-risk melanoma or a family history of the disease should discuss trial eligibility with their oncologist.

The broader lesson is one that the Indian medical establishment has been slow to absorb: cancer is not just a disease of treatment but of prevention and early detection. A vaccine that can eliminate residual disease after surgery is transformative. But it only works if the cancer is caught early enough for surgery to be an option in the first place.

**Sources:** Moderna/Merck ASCO 2026 press release; *Journal of Clinical Oncology* (June 2026); FDA breakthrough therapy designation announcement; *Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology* (2024)
